title: Ethnic Unity
paragraphs: It was a glorious hall, adorned with the portraits of illustrious Tamil kings, renowned poets and filled with audience eager to taste the manna of Tamil discourse. Vaḷavaṉ, a Tamil scholar and an intellectual with a broad forehead, penetrating eyes, slightly grey sprouting beard and blessed with ideas like an ever-flowing river, was lecturing on the title ‘Race’ (iṉam).*

The origin of various races in the world, the way they prospered, and the interaction and conflict between them were detailed with precision and historical evidences along with the researchers’ unambiguous views. Vaḷavaṉ’s discourse proved to be a feast as well as a medicine for the audience. “Now let me explain the rise and fall of our Tamil race”, announced Vaḷavaṉ after stealing a glance at the audience who were unconsciously drooping their heads like a bunch of lotus flowers in stooping posture due to the weight of their own petals.
Vaḷavaṉ spoke, “The Tamilians are one race, but Tamil itself constitutes three races. The speakers of the language form one race. How then is their language divided into three races?
Yes, gentlemen, what this humble man of yours states is an irrefutable truth! In our Tamil language the consonants could be divided into three races (categories):
k, c, ṭ, t, p, ṟ --> are vallinam (hard consonants)
ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m, ṉ --> are mellinam (soft consonants)
y, r, l, v, ḻ, ḷ --> are iṭaiyiṉam (medial consonants)
*The Tamil word iṉam, among others, means race, and a section or class of something. Here, the author plays pun on the meanings of this word.
Thus our Tamil consonants are divided into three classes. That is why I said, “The Tamilians are one race, while the Tamil language is of three races.”
After hearing this, a group of youth who were yet to be fully initiated into Tamil grammar stood up agitatedly and raised war-cries.
“What is this , sir? Wouldn’t our Tamil language’s fame get tarnished if her letters stand apart in three groups?”
An unperturbed Vaḷavaṉ’ came forward to allay their doubts in a balanced manner:

“Young men of valour! That you are apparently agitated with fears about the slight of the language makes me thrilled. But then, a five-footer like me would feel elated like a six-footer if you channelize your energy to oppose men smearing our Tamil language. You see, unlike the Tamil race, the Tamil language in her own characteristic style unites vallinam, mellinam and iṭaiyiṉam in itself and stands lofty.”

“Brothers! Sisters! In Tamil, /t/ is vallinam, /m/ is mellinam and /l/ iṭaiyiṉam. In this way, our classical Tamil language unites three diverse races of consonant letters to make a harmonious whole. But then, the practitioners of the Tamil language are split into various groups and stand apart. Do think about this. When vallinam, mellinam and iṭaiyiṉam blend together and make a lustrous entity called Tamil, is this correct on the part of the Tamilians to be divided into so many groups?”

The gathering dispersed and the youth took leave of each other after discussing among themselves, this nagging question: “When the word Tamil is formed by the blending of letters from three different classes, should the Tamil race stand divided?” There was only a deep sigh.

> /k/, /c/, /ṭ/, /t/, /p/ and /ṟ/ are called hard consonants. > /ṅ/, /ñ/, /ṇ/, /n/, /m/ and /ṉ/ are called soft consonants. > /y/, /r/, /l/, /v/, /ḻ/ and /ḷ/ are called medial consonants. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Nūl Marapu, verses 19, 20 and 21)
